excerptPointers.summary: An opening invocation of self and reader, asserting the equivalence of the speaker's atoms with the reader's.
A child asks what the grass is, and the speaker offers cumulative metaphors that range across class, race, and mortality.

excerptPointers.section: Because I could not stop for Death
excerptPointers.summary: A short lyric in which the speaker rides in a carriage with personified Death, passing scenes of childhood, harvest, and a setting sun.

excerptPointers.section: Tell all the truth but tell it slant
excerptPointers.summary: A compact poem arguing that truth must be approached indirectly so that its brilliance does not blind the recipient.
Two women remain in the Wright kitchen while the men investigate elsewhere; the stage directions and dialogue draw attention to small domestic details the men dismiss.

excerptPointers.section: The discovery of the bird cage
excerptPointers.summary: Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters notice a broken bird cage and reflect on what its condition might suggest about the household.
An African American family in the Northern United States is introduced through warm domestic dialogue; the title character expresses her love of children.
Rachel's mother discloses the racial violence that shaped the family's past, prompting Rachel to reconsider her future.
The narrator characterizes Gabriel Oak through his Sunday demeanor and his daily one, drawing inferences about temperament from outward signs.
Gabriel and Bathsheba labor through the night to protect ricks of grain from a coming storm; the narration alternates between the natural world and human endurance.
Gurov observes a young woman walking with a small dog; the narration sketches his routine cynicism alongside the new acquaintance.
Gurov returns to his life in Moscow expecting to forget Anna; the narration tracks the dissonance between his outward routine and his interior preoccupation.

author: Katherine Mansfield
title: The Garden Party and Other Stories

excerptPointers.summary: Laura inspects the lawn and instructs the workmen setting up a marquee; her impressions of the men complicate her family's class assumptions.
After the party, Laura takes leftovers to the home of a working-class family who have suffered a death; the contrast unsettles her composure.
A poem that examines the genre of poetry itself, suggesting that authentic poems must contain real material rather than mere ornament.
A short poem describing marine creatures and a battered cliff, organized around precise visual imagery and a tightly patterned syllabic stanza.
The narrator consults a medical reference and convinces himself he suffers from every disease listed except housemaid's knee, in a comic register.
The narrator describes the chaos of packing for a river trip, using a tone that mocks both his own competence and that of his companions.
Enslaved characters communicate news of the Civil War's progress through a coded conversation about marketing produce.
Iola argues for a particular vision of African American education in conversation with friends and family after the war.
A porch full of townspeople observe and comment on a confrontation between two men, with the narration shifting between collective voice and individual speech.
After Joe's death, a bobcat appears at the sawmill; the townspeople interpret the animal's presence in folkloric terms.
The narrator describes the Nebraska prairie in winter, characterizing the land as resistant to settlement and indifferent to the settlers' efforts.
Alexandra Bergson explains to her brothers why the family should buy more land rather than sell out, using observational evidence about the soil and neighbors.
An outsider narrator recounts arriving in Starkfield and forming an impression of Ethan Frome from glimpses around the village.
Ethan and Mattie agree to sled down a hill; the narration interweaves their physical descent with their decision-making.

excerptPointers.section: Departure from the house of Shaws
excerptPointers.summary: David Balfour leaves his uncle's home; the narration shifts from suspicion at the house to anticipation about the journey ahead.
After being kidnapped, David is held aboard a brig and meets Alan Breck Stewart; their alliance forms under pressure from the crew.
The poet addresses a divine listener and reflects on the renewal of the self as an instrument for song.

excerptPointers.section: Where the mind is without fear
excerptPointers.summary: A short poem that catalogs conditions for an awakened nation and culminates in a prayer for clarity of thought.
The narrator records his sudden suspicion that everyone around him intends harm, beginning with an observation of the moon and the dog at the gate.
The narrator examines historical texts and concludes that the words of Confucian morality conceal a different message.
An anonymous narrator describes a yawl anchored on the Thames at dusk; Marlow begins his story with a reflection on London's own past as a place at the edge of empire.
Marlow describes his arrival at a colonial station, observing the disjunction between official accounting and the visible suffering of laborers.
A guest produces a manuscript at a Christmas gathering; the narration sets up the story of the governess as a document with multiple layers of mediation.
The governess sees a figure on the parapet of Bly; the narration tracks her shifting interpretations of what she has seen.
A boy describes the dead-end street where he lives and the priest who once occupied his house, establishing the texture of his neighborhood.
Gabriel watches snow fall over Ireland from a hotel window after his wife reveals a memory; the prose moves from interior reflection to a wide aerial view.
The narrator describes the upstairs nursery she has been assigned, including its barred windows and patterned wallpaper, in a tone that mixes observation and unease.
The narrator describes how the wallpaper appears different by moonlight; the entry tracks her growing identification with what she perceives behind the pattern.
Mrs. Spring Fragrance is introduced through her interactions with American neighbors; the narration registers small misunderstandings of language and custom.
Mrs. Spring Fragrance writes a letter from a trip to San Francisco; her observations on a lecture about American romance complicate her husband's traditional views.
The narrator describes the Smith family's boarding house in late nineteenth-century Boston, with attention to its boarders and the social texture of the neighborhood.
A character delivers a speech at a community meeting addressing political conditions for African Americans; the narration captures audience reaction.

excerptPointers.section: John and Annie at the plantation
excerptPointers.summary: A Northern couple considers buying a former plantation; Uncle Julius offers a tale that bears on their decision.
Uncle Julius narrates an embedded story involving a conjure woman; the narration alternates between the embedded tale and its frame.

author: James Weldon Johnson
title: The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man

excerptPointers.summary: The narrator describes the moment in school when a teacher's question forces a sudden reconsideration of his racial identity.
The narrator describes hearing ragtime piano performed in a New York club, analyzing the formal qualities that distinguish the music.
A short lyric describing a public face that conceals interior pain; the poem uses repeated rhyme to enact concealment.
The poem extends a sustained metaphor of a caged bird to articulate longing for freedom.

author: Sarah Orne Jewett
title: The Country of the Pointed Firs

excerptPointers.summary: A summer visitor describes settling into a rented room with Mrs. Todd in a Maine coastal village; the prose attends to herbs, weather, and small social signs.
The narrator and Mrs. Todd sail to visit Mrs. Todd's mother on a small island; the scene develops slow exposition through ordinary tasks.
A first-person epitaph spoken by a long-lived woman who recalls a life of work, dance, and child-rearing in a Midwestern town.
An opening poem cataloging the residents of a graveyard through repeated questions, establishing the collection's premise.
Mrs. Hale rides to a neighbor's farmhouse with the sheriff's wife and reflects on what she has and has not done as a neighbor.
The two women examine a quilt and notice irregular stitches in one block; their observation prompts a private decision about what to share with the men.

author: Walt Whitman
title: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd

excerptPointers.summary: An elegy opens with the recurrence of lilacs and a western star; the speaker sets up three image-clusters that will return throughout the poem.
An embedded song addresses death directly, framing it as a soothing presence; the section sits within the poem's larger structure of elegy.

excerptPointers.section: There's a certain Slant of light
excerptPointers.summary: A short poem in which winter afternoon light is given a metaphysical weight; the speaker compares the light's effect to a wound and a seal.
The speaker recounts the moment of dying as a small auditory disturbance interposed between observers and the deathbed.
Emerson advances his central claim that each person should rely on the authority of their own intuition rather than imitate others.
Emerson argues that society conspires against the self-reliance of its members and contrasts the original mind with the conforming one.

excerptPointers.section: Why I went to the woods
excerptPointers.summary: Thoreau states his reasons for moving to Walden Pond and explains his program of deliberate living.
Thoreau describes the sounds that reach his cabin from a railroad and the surrounding woods, drawing observations about labor and time.

author: Mary Wollstonecraft
title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

excerptPointers.summary: Wollstonecraft frames her central claim that women's perceived inferiority is the result of inadequate education rather than inherent capacity.
Wollstonecraft examines Rousseau's claims about female education in Émile and argues against his prescriptions point by point.
Cooper argues that the elevation of African American women is essential to the progress of the race and the nation.
Cooper develops a case for women's higher education by examining historical examples and contemporary objections.

author: Ida B. Wells
title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases

excerptPointers.summary: Wells assembles statistics on lynchings and shows how widely reported reasons for the killings fail to match the documented record.

excerptPointers.section: The Black and White of It
excerptPointers.summary: Wells examines press coverage of specific cases and argues that the standard narrative used to justify lynching does not survive scrutiny of the underlying facts.

excerptPointers.section: Lecture I: On the Nature of Knowledge
excerptPointers.summary: Wright argues that knowledge is not the property of any class but the inheritance of all who can be taught to inquire.
Wright defends free inquiry against social pressure, treating dogmatic authority as incompatible with civic life.
Keller defines an inward optimism that develops from the discipline of meeting external limits with sustained effort.
Keller turns from a definition of optimism to its public consequences, considering the role of optimism in social reform.
Du Bois introduces the concept of double consciousness and reflects on the experience of identity in post-Reconstruction America.
Du Bois examines the spirituals as historical documents and as art, considering what they preserve of African American experience.

author: William James
title: Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking

excerptPointers.section: Lecture I: The Present Dilemma in Philosophy
excerptPointers.summary: James opens by sketching what he calls a temperamental conflict in philosophy between tender-minded and tough-minded positions.
James uses an anecdote about people disputing whether a man circles a squirrel to illustrate how the pragmatic method dissolves verbal disagreements.

author: William Hazlitt
title: Table-Talk: Essays on Men and Manners

excerptPointers.summary: Hazlitt reflects on the experience of working in oils and what painting teaches about attention.
Hazlitt distinguishes plain and ornamented prose styles and argues that what looks easy in writing requires careful selection.
Hearn records his first impressions on landing in Japan and describes the sensory texture of the streets and shop signs.
Hearn visits a small shrine in a rural area and records local practices, with reflections on what they suggest about communal memory.

author: Walter Pater
title: The Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry

excerptPointers.summary: Pater defines the role of the aesthetic critic as one who isolates what is distinctive in a work and analyzes the conditions under which it produces its effect.
Pater closes by arguing for an attentive engagement with experience and characterizes the moments at which life becomes acute.

author: Pearl S. Buck
title: East and West and the Novel

excerptPointers.summary: Pearl S. Buck's mature work is not yet in US public domain; this entry is retained for tracking but should not be selected for excerpt generation until rights status changes.
Martineau lays out the program for her study of American institutions, distinguishing her approach from earlier travel writing.
Martineau examines the legal and economic conditions of women in the United States and contrasts them with the rhetoric of equality found in public documents.

author: Lucy Stone
title: Address to the Massachusetts Constitutional Convention

excerptPointers.summary: Stone argues for the inclusion of women in the franchise on the basis of consent-of-the-governed principles, addressing delegates directly.
Stone closes by inviting delegates to consider the consistency of their stated principles with the law as currently constituted.

author: Frederick Douglass
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

excerptPointers.summary: Douglass recounts how Mrs. Auld began teaching him the alphabet and how her husband intervened, treating literacy as a threat to the institution of slavery.
Douglass narrates his physical resistance against the overseer Covey and reflects on the change this confrontation produced in him.

author: Harriet Jacobs
title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl

excerptPointers.summary: Jacobs describes the small attic crawlspace where she hid for seven years to evade her owner, attending to the physical conditions of the hiding place.
Jacobs addresses Northern readers directly, acknowledging the difficulty of her testimony and asserting its truth.
Antin recounts the family's voyage from Polotzk and their arrival in Boston, comparing the small details of each setting.
Antin describes her first weeks of public school in Boston and the language acquisition that accompanied her early academic success.
Truth describes her decision to walk away from her enslaver before her legally promised emancipation date and her reflections on what would constitute a just departure.
Truth narrates her legal effort to recover her son, who had been illegally sold across state lines, including her interactions with sympathetic Quakers.

author: Black Hawk
title: Autobiography of Ma-ka-tai-me-she-kia-kiak, or Black Hawk

excerptPointers.summary: Black Hawk describes the community life of his Sauk village along the Rock River and details its agricultural and ceremonial calendar.
Black Hawk presents his account of the 1804 treaty and explains why he and his people did not consider its terms binding on the Sauk nation.

author: Olaudah Equiano
title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano

excerptPointers.summary: Equiano describes the village life and customs of his early childhood before his capture, attending to family and community organization.
Equiano recounts the conditions aboard the slave ship and the sensory disorientation of the voyage in language addressed to a European readership.
Mill describes the intensive education his father designed for him and reflects on what it provided and what it omitted.
Mill describes a period of depression in his early twenties and examines what reading Wordsworth contributed to his recovery.
Adams compares the influences of his grandfather's house at Quincy with his family's Boston residence, treating the two as opposing principles in his early life.
Adams visits the Paris Exposition and reflects on the symbolic difference between the medieval cult of the Virgin and the modern dynamo.

author: Charlotte Forten Grimké
title: The Journal of Charlotte L. Forten

excerptPointers.summary: Forten records her studies at the Higginson Grammar School in Salem and her readings outside school in works of history and poetry.
Forten records her observations as a teacher among formerly enslaved people on the Sea Islands during the Civil War.
Gorky describes the household of his grandfather, including the daily violence and the dyeing-shop labor that punctuated family life.
The narrator recalls his grandmother's evening stories and the impression her speech and gestures left on him as a child.

excerptPointers.section: Letter to T. W. Higginson, April 1862
excerptPointers.summary: Dickinson writes to Higginson asking whether he considers her verse alive, and characterizes her own habits of reading and composition.
Dickinson writes to her sister-in-law with a description of the household and a brief reflection on a recent reading.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: The Correspondence of Thomas Carlyle and Ralph Waldo Emerson

excerptPointers.section: Early letters from Emerson to Carlyle
excerptPointers.summary: Emerson writes to Carlyle about the reception of Sartor Resartus in America and about arrangements for an American edition.
Emerson responds to Carlyle's manuscript and describes the experience of reading the work over multiple sessions.
Douglass addresses his former enslaver directly in an open letter and explains his reasons for breaking the customary silence between an enslaved person and an enslaver.
Douglass invites Auld to consider how he would respond if his own daughter were subjected to what enslaved daughters routinely faced.
Keats writes to his brothers and articulates his concept of negative capability through brief reflections on Shakespeare and Coleridge.
Keats writes to Fanny Brawne during his illness and describes the routine of his confinement and his uncertain recovery.
Van Gogh writes to his brother about his work in Arles and the role of complementary colors in the canvases he is producing.

excerptPointers.section: On the role of the artist
excerptPointers.summary: Van Gogh reflects on what he wants his paintings to communicate to ordinary viewers and contrasts this aim with academic painting.

author: Emily Dickinson
title: Because I could not stop for Death

author: Robert Frost
title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening

excerptPointers.summary: Tropical fruit in a New York shop window stirs the speaker's memories of home and ends in a wave of longing and tears.

author: William Wordsworth
title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

excerptPointers.summary: The speaker, wandering alone, comes suddenly upon a vast crowd of daffodils beside a lake.

_meta.quoteVerify: Quoted verbatim from the 1815 revised text as printed in standard Wordsworth editions (Poems, in Two Volumes, 1807; rev. 1815): 'I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills, / When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host, of golden daffodils; / Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.' Stanza 2 as in the 1815 text ('Continuous as the stars that shine...'). Public domain; used in test8 q05.

excerptPointers.summary: The speaker resolves to leave for the island of Innisfree, imagines the solitary life there, and reveals that its sounds reach him on the city pavements.

_meta.quoteVerify: Quoted verbatim from the standard text (first collected in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892; written 1888, first published in the National Observer, 1890): 'I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree...' through '...I hear it in the deep heart's core.' Public domain; used in test8 q32.

author: William Hazlitt
title: On Going a Journey
collection: Table-Talk: Essays on Men and Manners (1821)

excerptPointers.summary: The pleasure of journeying alone: society indoors, nature as company out of doors, liberty as the soul of a journey.
A general declaration ('I hear America singing') elaborated through a catalog of workers, each singing at a characteristic task.

author: Frederick II
title: De arte venandi cum avibus
collection: medieval manuscript tradition; standard English translation: The Art of Falconry (Wood & Fyfe, 1943)

excerptPointers.section: referenced as a topical work, not excerpted
excerptPointers.summary: Frederick II's falconry treatise (c. 1245), notable for testing received claims (barnacle-goose legend, vulture senses) against observation.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
title: The Tide Rises, the Tide Falls

excerptPointers.summary: Three refrain-linked stanzas move from twilight to night to morning; the traveler vanishes while the tide's rhythm persists.

notes: Public-domain; verified against Wikisource text of Ultima Thule.

author: Sara Teasdale
title: There Will Come Soft Rains
collection: Flame and Shadow (1920); first published in Harper's Monthly Magazine, July 1918

excerptPointers.summary: A catalog of spring images turns to the assertion that nature would neither notice nor mourn humanity's disappearance.

notes: Public-domain (pre-1930 publication); verified against Wikisource text of Flame and Shadow.

excerptPointers.summary: From her window the speaker watches the lamplit street, contrasts the moon with the city glare, and sides with the moon in an alien city.
An ideal summer morning before a garden party: perfect weather, dawn-mown lawns, roses in abundance.

author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
title: Sympathy
collection: Lyrics of the Hearthside (1899); text as printed in The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar (1913)

excerptPointers.summary: The speaker knows what the caged bird feels amid spring, why it beats its wing on the bars, and why its song is a prayer rather than a carol of joy.

author: Emily Brontë
title: Spellbound
collection: Written November 1837; published posthumously (also known by its first line, 'The night is darkening round me')

excerptPointers.summary: A storm intensifies stanza by stanza while the speaker repeats that she cannot go; the final line turns compulsion into choice: 'I will not, cannot go.'

author: Elizabeth Gaskell
title: Cranford

excerptPointers.section: Chapter I, Our Society (the rules for visiting)
excerptPointers.summary: The narrator sets out the visiting rules of a small English town governed by its older women and reports the effects of obeying them.

notes: Verified full text at Project Gutenberg (ebook 394). Gaskell died 1865; first published 1853 — US public domain.

author: Mark Twain
title: Life on the Mississippi

excerptPointers.section: Chapter 9, reading the face of the water
excerptPointers.summary: The narrator describes learning to read the river as a text and weighs the skill he gained against the beauty he stopped seeing.

notes: Verified full text at Project Gutenberg (ebook 245). First published 1883 — US public domain.

author: Alice Dunbar-Nelson
title: M’sieu Fortier’s Violin

excerptPointers.section: Opening: the last man out of the French Opera
excerptPointers.summary: An elderly first violinist leaves the opera house and the narrator sketches the quiet routine of his life and what his work asks of him.

notes: Story in The Goodness of St. Rocque, and Other Stories (1899); verified full text at Project Gutenberg (ebook 688). Author died 1935; work published 1899 — US public domain.

author: John Keats
title: To Autumn

excerptPointers.summary: A three-stanza ode addressing autumn directly, picturing the season first as ripening force, then as a figure resting amid the harvest, then as its own music.

notes: Text from Keats: Poems Published in 1820, Project Gutenberg ebook 23684. Published 1820 — US public domain.

author: Robert Browning
title: My Last Duchess

excerptPointers.summary: A duke shows an envoy the portrait of his late wife and, while describing the painting, betrays his resentment of her evenhanded gratitude.

notes: Text from Browning’s Shorter Poems, Project Gutenberg ebook 16376. First published in Dramatic Lyrics, 1842 — US public domain.

author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
title: The Poet and His Song

excerptPointers.summary: Four stanzas in which the speaker names the hardships of his farming life and answers each of them with the refrain that he sings and all is well.

notes: Poem first collected in Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896); text verified in The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar, Project Gutenberg ebook 18338 — US public domain. CB official item e662866f quotes the first stanza verbatim — do not quote this poem in authored items.

author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
title: A New England Nun

excerptPointers.section: Opening: Louisa Ellis at her supper
excerptPointers.summary: A woman who has lived alone for years puts away her sewing, picks currants, and lays a careful table for one; the narrator dwells on the exactness of every habit.

notes: Collected in A New England Nun and Other Stories (1891); full text transcribed at Wikisource. Freeman died 1930; the story was published 1891 — US public domain.
